::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives" icon="false"}
After this lecture (and Lab 5) you can:

1. **formalize** conjunctive and path queries over an incomplete KG, and explain with numbers why answering them is not chained lookup;
2. **explain** query embedding — Query2box's projection and intersection on boxes, why regions rather than points, and (statement level) how BetaE buys negation;
3. **evaluate** multi-hop reasoning without fooling yourself: easy versus hard answers, entity leakage, and metrics that measure inference rather than recall;
4. **describe** the GraphRAG pattern and argue, per question type, when structured retrieval beats vector similarity — and when it loses;
5. **sketch** LLM-assisted KG construction and name its three failure modes with their repairs.
:::

## The question that is a path

Begin with the questions this week exists to answer. A pharmacologist asks:
*"which drugs target a protein associated with this inflammation pathway?"* A compliance analyst asks: *"which companies are owned by subsidiaries
of sanctioned entities?"* A student registering for next semester asks: *"which
courses are prerequisites of prerequisites of this one?"* None of these questions is a fact — each is a **path with a
variable in the middle**, marching hop by hop through a knowledge graph that Week 4
taught you to regard with suspicion: incomplete at every single hop.

Notice also what kind of questions these are, sociologically: they are the
*valuable* ones. Single-fact lookups — a capital, a birth year — are cheap precisely
because they are stated somewhere; multi-hop questions are where analysis happens,
because their answers are *implied* by the record without appearing in it — no
document lists "companies owned by subsidiaries of sanctioned entities", which is
exactly why a compliance analyst is paid to derive the list. The pattern generalizes:
drug discovery, intelligence analysis, supply-chain risk, curriculum planning — in
each, the question's worth is proportional to the number of hops between what is
written and what is asked. Week 4 built a machine for one hop. Today's problem is
that value lives at two hops and beyond, and one-hop machines, chained naively,
decay there — by exactly how much, you are about to predict.

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** Suppose single-hop completion is quite good: each hop of a
query independently succeeds with probability 0.9. What is the chance a 3-hop chained
answer is right — and, harder: if the first hop has ~100 candidate answers you must
enumerate before taking the second hop, how many candidate paths is a 3-hop query
juggling?

::: {.predict-answer}
$0.9^3 \approx 0.73$ — chaining turns a good single-hop model into a coin-flippy
multi-hop one, and errors *compound silently*. And $\sim 100^2 = 10{,}000$ intermediate
paths for just three hops: enumeration explodes exponentially in query depth. These two
numbers — compounding error and blowing-up frontier — are the entire case for this
week's idea: don't chain answers, **embed the question**.
:::
:::

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w5-hero.html >}}

The figure's dashed edge is Week 4's open-world assumption coming home: Naproxen *does*
target COX-2 in the world (it is an NSAID like its neighbors), but nobody wrote it
down — so the traversal answer is not wrong, it is *incomplete in exactly the way the
graph is*, and it fails silently: nothing about the returned set announces a member
is missing. A query answerer worth deploying must complete *while it walks*.

**Roadmap.** (1) Queries, formalized — the shape taxonomy, and the two quantitative
ways chaining dies. (2) The week's big idea: queries as geometric regions,
Query2box's operators with worked numbers, what boxes can and cannot close over, and
the search-based rival. (3) Evaluation that separates inference from memorization.
(4) The LLM era, part one: GraphRAG — structure as a retrieval index for language
models, with the full pipeline anatomy. (5) Part two: language models as KG
builders, the three failures, and the three-pattern map of the whole KG×LLM space.
Plus: the **course project launches today**.

::: {.callout-note title="Recap — what this lecture assumes" collapse="true"}
- **Week 4**: triples, the open-world assumption, completion-as-ranking, filtered
  metrics, and the corollary that geometric one-hop models cannot represent
  transitivity exactly — this week is what you do about it.
- **Week 2**: Louvain/Leiden community detection — it returns, of all places, inside

- **Week 3**: embedding-space reasoning; Pitfall 1 (leakage through the data pipeline)

## 1. Queries, formalized — and the two ways chaining dies

The queries above are
<span class="term" data-def="Conjunctive query: an existentially quantified conjunction of triple patterns, e.g. q(D) = ∃P: assoc(P, Inflammation) ∧ targets(D, P). The bread and butter of database query languages — and of this lecture.">**conjunctive queries**</span>:
existential variables, triple patterns, one free variable whose bindings are the
answers. Write the hero query as
$$
q(D) \;=\; \exists P:\; \textit{assoc}(P, \text{Inflammation}) \,\wedge\, \textit{targets}(D, P),
$$
and read it aloud once, because the notation earns its keep only if it stays
attached to meaning: "the answers are the drugs $D$ for which *there exists* some
protein $P$ — we do not care which — that is associated with Inflammation and
targeted by $D$." The existential is the crux: the query never asks you to *name*
the intermediate protein, only to be confident one exists, and that is exactly the
looseness that lets embedding methods skip enumerating it. Draw the query as a
**computation DAG**: anchor → relation edge → variable → relation edge → answer
variable. Intersections appear when two branches constrain the same variable; unions
and negation extend the language (and will stress our geometry). Databases have
answered such queries for fifty years — SPARQL would dispatch the hero query in
milliseconds — so be precise about what is *new* here: the database's contract is
"answers entailed by stored facts", flawless and complete relative to the store,
and mute about everything the store forgot. Our contract is "answers plausible
given the stored facts" — weaker, riskier, and the only one that can say
*Naproxen*. Both contracts have customers; this lecture is about serving the second
without lying about which contract you are under.

The query language this machinery targets has a name and a taxonomy, and both are
worth owning because every paper in this literature speaks them. The class is
**EPFO** queries — Existential Positive First-Order: conjunction, disjunction, and
$\exists$, but no negation and no universal quantifier (each exclusion will earn its
explanation today). Within it, the field standardized on nine query *shapes*, named
by their DAGs: the **path family** — `1p` (plain completion: one anchor, one hop —
all of Week 4 was this shape), `2p`, `3p` (longer chains, our hero is a `2p`); the
**intersection family** — `2i`, `3i` (two or three 1-hop branches meeting at the
answer: "proteins associated with Inflammation AND targeted by Aspirin"); the
**mixed shapes** — `ip` (intersect, then project onward: "drugs targeting [the
proteins in both pathways]") and `pi` (project along one branch, intersect with
another); and the **union shapes** `2u`, `up`. Training conventionally sees only
five shapes (`1p 2p 3p 2i 3i`); the rest are evaluated zero-shot, because the entire
bet of query embedding is that *operators*, not query shapes, are what gets learned
— learn projection and intersection well, and `ip` compiles out of parts the model
has never seen assembled. That compositional bet, incidentally, is the same one
language modeling makes about syntax, and its success here predates its fame there.

Unions deserve their promised one paragraph now rather than a footnote later,
because the trick is used verbatim in production systems. Any EPFO query can be
rewritten into **disjunctive normal form** — a union of purely conjunctive queries —
by the distributive law, so a system that handles conjunctive shapes handles unions
by embedding each branch separately and scoring an entity by its *best* branch
(minimum distance over branches). Worked micro-example: "drugs for Inflammation
**or** Diabetes" becomes two `2p` branches — one anchored at each disease — and
Metformin, hopeless in the Inflammation branch, enters the answer set through the
Diabetes branch's box. The costs are honest: DNF can blow up exponentially for
deeply nested unions (rare in practice), and "min over branches" quietly assumes
branch scores are comparable — which trained models mostly deliver and nothing
guarantees. Keep the rewrite in your pocket; it converts every union question about
this lecture into a conjunction question.

On a *complete* graph, answering is database technology — subgraph matching, done.
On a real KG, chaining one-hop steps dies twice, as your prediction computed:
**compounding error** (each hop multiplies its own miss probability — a good model
becomes a bad pipeline) and **frontier explosion** (enumerating intermediate
candidates costs $O(b^k)$ for branching $b$ and depth $k$ — and to be robust you must
keep *low-scoring* candidates too, making $b$ large). The fix must avoid enumerating
intermediates altogether.

Watch both modes run — strict traversal, then completion-aware answering:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w5-query.html >}}

The widget's soft mode is deliberately the *crudest* possible completion-aware
answerer — threshold a Week-4 scorer per hop — and it already surfaces the design
questions the rest of the lecture answers properly. How confident must an unstated
edge be to cross the threshold, and who calibrates that? (Nobody can, under the open
world — §2 sidesteps thresholds entirely by ranking.) Should hop two trust hop one's
soft additions as firmly as its stated facts? (The widget does; principled methods
carry the softness forward instead.) And where does the compute go as queries deepen?
(The widget scores candidates per hop — the frontier again; §2's whole point is
refusing to do that.) A crude baseline that provokes the right questions is worth
more than a polished one that hides them; keep this trick for your own projects.

## 2. Queries as regions: Query2box

Here is the move, and it is Week 3's move aimed at a new target: we embedded nodes,
then facts — now **embed the query itself**. Process the computation DAG left to
right, but in embedding space: the anchor is its entity embedding; each relation
application is a learned **operator** on the query's representation; and when the DAG
is consumed, the answers are simply *the entities near the final representation*. No
intermediate entities are ever enumerated — depth costs a matrix op, not a
combinatorial frontier.

Pause on how strange and how disciplined this is. Strange: the object being embedded
is not a thing in the world but a *sentence about* the world — a logical formula gets
coordinates, and its geometric neighborhood *is* its answer set. Disciplined: it is
still nothing but the filing cabinet, filled in one more time. Encoder: anchor
lookup composed with learned operators (the first non-table encoder of the semester,
one week before GNNs make that upgrade everywhere). Decoder: distance from an entity
to the query's region. Similarity: query–answer pairs sampled from the graph. Loss:
the same margin-vs-corruption shape as Week 4, with corrupted *answers* as
negatives. Every skill you have — negative-sampling hygiene, filtered ranking,
leakage paranoia — transfers without modification, which is exactly why the course
built the cabinet before building this. And note what trained operators buy that
Week 4's per-fact scores cannot: the *composition* of two projections is computed
inside the space, so the error of hop two conditions on the *soft* output of hop
one rather than on a hard, possibly-wrong intermediate decision — the arithmetic
reason the $0.9^3$ compounding from the predict block does not apply.

One design question remains: what *kind* of object should a query's representation be?
A point fails for a reason you can state precisely: a query with many answers needs a
representation that many entities can be simultaneously close to — and a point picks
favorites. Query2box (2020) answers: an axis-aligned **box** — center $\mathbf{c}$,
offset $\mathbf{o}$, containing everything within $\mathbf{o}$ of $\mathbf{c}$
coordinatewise:

- **Projection** (apply relation $r$): $\mathbf{c} \mathrel{+}= \mathbf{c}_r$,
  $\mathbf{o} \mathrel{+}= \mathbf{o}_r$ — the box *translates* (Week 4's TransE
  instinct) and *grows* (following a relation can only widen the answer set: a
  disease has some associated proteins, those proteins have *more* targeting drugs —
  monotone growth is a logical fact about existential queries, and the operator
  hard-codes it);
- **Intersection** (two branches meet): the new center is an attention-weighted
  average, the new offset shrinks below each input's — answer sets can only narrow.
  Why attention rather than the plain mean? Branches are not equally informative — a
  tight box ("proteins in this rare pathway") should pull the meet toward itself
  against a loose one ("things associated with Inflammation") — so the weights are
  computed from the branch representations, the first self-attention this course has
  met, one week before it becomes a habit;
- **Score**: distance from an entity to the box — zero-ish inside, growing outside,
  with the inside term down-weighted so the box interior is genuinely "in" (the
  worked numbers below make both regimes concrete).

Training mirrors Week 4 so closely you could write it from memory: sample queries
from the training graph by instantiating the shape templates, take their
training-reachable answers as positives, corrupt answers into negatives, apply a
margin. The one novelty is what "parameters" means now — besides the entity table,
each relation owns its projection vectors, and the intersection network is *shared
across all queries* — so the operator learns from every intersection in the corpus,
a first taste of the parameter-sharing medicine that Week 6 prescribes for
everything.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w5-boxes.html >}}

The figure's quiet miracle deserves noise: **Naproxen is inside the answer box** even
though its edge was never stated. Training placed Naproxen near the other COX drugs
(their stated edges overlap), and the region swallowed it. The box did not *look up*
the answer — it *generalized* to it, which is precisely what §1 demanded.

Run the scoring arithmetic once on the figure's actual coordinates, because "distance
to a box" hides two regimes worth feeling in your fingers. The distance is
$d(\mathbf{v}) = \|\max(|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{c}| - \mathbf{o},\, 0)\|_1 + \alpha\,\|\min(|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{c}|,\, \mathbf{o})\|_1$
— an *outside* term that only fires beyond the walls, plus a discounted *inside*
term that gently ranks the interior. Take the answer box at center
$\mathbf{c} = (5.7, 5.6)$ with offsets $\mathbf{o} = (1.3, 1.4)$, and $\alpha = 0.2$.
Ibuprofen at $(6.1, 4.9)$: deviations $(0.4, 0.7)$, both under the offsets — outside
term $0$, inside term $0.2 \times 1.1 = 0.22$. Metformin at $(1.5, 1.6)$: deviations
$(4.2, 4.0)$, exceeding the offsets by $(2.9, 2.6)$ — outside term $5.5$, plus the
saturated inside term $0.2 \times 2.7 = 0.54$, total $6.04$. A twenty-seven-fold
score separation between an inside answer and an outside non-answer, produced by a
formula you can differentiate — and the reason $\alpha < 1$ exists is now visible:
with $\alpha = 0$ every interior point ties at zero and training gets no signal to
center the box on its answers; with $\alpha = 1$ the walls stop mattering and the
box degenerates back into a point scorer. The lab's first exercise makes you compute
exactly these two cases by hand before any training happens.

::: {#prp-closure .proposition name="What boxes close over — and what they don't"}
The intersection of two axis-aligned boxes is an axis-aligned box (possibly empty),
so conjunction stays inside the representation. The **union** of two boxes is in
general *not* a box, and the **complement** of a box is never one — so disjunction
and negation leave the representation class.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (one line each, plus what the field did about it)</summary>
Intersection: per coordinate, the meet of two intervals is an interval —
$[\max(l_1, l_2), \min(h_1, h_2)]$ — and a product of intervals is a box. Union: two
disjoint boxes' union is disconnected; boxes are connected. Complement: unbounded,
boxes are bounded. Workarounds: Query2box handles unions by rewriting queries into
**disjunctive normal form** — a union of purely conjunctive branches, each embedded as
its own box, scored by the minimum distance over branches. Negation needed a new
geometry: **BetaE** replaces boxes with Beta distributions per coordinate, where
complement is the parameter swap $(\alpha, \beta) \to (\beta, \alpha)$ — a
representation *chosen because* the logical operator becomes cheap. The design lesson
outlives both papers: pick the geometry after you list the operators. $\square$
</details>

{{< include ../assets/d3/w5-boxes.html >}}

Two postscripts complete the query-embedding picture — one geometric, one
contrarian. The geometric one: BetaE's move deserves a concrete image beyond
"parameter swap". Each coordinate of a query becomes a **Beta distribution** on
$[0, 1]$ — a bump whose shape two parameters $(\alpha, \beta)$ control — and an
entity is scored by how well its own per-coordinate bumps align (KL divergence).
Negation flips $(\alpha, \beta)$ to $(\beta, \alpha)$, which literally mirrors the
bump: mass near 0 becomes mass near 1 — "definitely has this property" becomes
"definitely lacks it" — and, unlike the complement of a box, the mirror of a Beta
*is* a Beta. Intersection multiplies densities (both constraints must be probable),
which is again closed. The uniform distribution is a fixed point of negation —
"unknown" negated is "unknown" — an elegant little homage to the open-world
assumption baked into the geometry itself. That is twice now that this lecture's
slogan has cashed out: *list your operators, then buy the geometry that closes over
them.*

The contrarian postscript: query embedding is not the only survivor of §1's
massacre, and the strongest alternative — **CQD** (continuous query decomposition) —
is philosophically its opposite. CQD keeps Week 4's plain one-hop scorer and answers
multi-hop queries at *inference time* by treating the query as a fuzzy-logic
optimization: find intermediate entities maximizing a t-norm combination (soft AND)
of the one-hop scores, via beam search over top-$k$ candidates per hop. No query
training at all — and on many benchmarks it *beats* trained query embeddings, at the
price of the beam's exponential appetite for deep queries. The design tension is a
useful permanent lens: Query2box amortizes reasoning into geometry (train hard,
answer in one distance computation); CQD spends at query time and keeps the model
simple. Amortize versus search — you will meet this trade again in every corner of
ML systems, usually with worse names.

## 3. Grading a reasoner without grading its memory

Multi-hop evaluation has a failure mode beyond Week 4's, and most published numbers
have stepped in it at least once. For a test query, split its true answers:

- **easy answers** — reachable by pure traversal of the *training* graph. A system
  can find these with zero inference: they are lookups wearing a costume;
- **hard answers** — requiring at least one edge held out of training. Only these
  measure generalization.

Report metrics on **hard answers only** (this is the Query2box protocol), and
filtered, as always — where filtering for queries means masking *all other known
answers* (easy and hard alike) when ranking each one. Work one query through the full
protocol, because the bookkeeping is exactly where implementations go wrong. Suppose
a `2p` test query has easy answers $\{e_1, e_2\}$ and hard answers $\{h_1, h_2\}$, and
the model's ranking of all entities places them at raw positions
$e_1{=}1,\, e_2{=}3,\, h_1{=}4,\, h_2{=}9$. Scoring $h_1$: mask $e_1, e_2, h_2$ —
three known answers sit at positions above or below — leaving $h_1$ at filtered rank
$2$ (only the position-2 non-answer outranks it). Scoring $h_2$: mask the other
three, filtered rank $6$. Hard-answer MRR: $\tfrac12(\tfrac12 + \tfrac16) = \tfrac13$;
the easy answers contribute *nothing* to the headline — they are graded separately,
as the sanity channel. Two conventions to notice: every hard answer is scored (not
just the best one — a query with many hard answers is many test items), and the
easy/hard label is a property of the *answer*, not the query, since one query
routinely has both kinds (ours did).

The literature's vocabulary for the two channels is worth adopting:
**entailment** — retrieving answers the training graph logically contains (easy) —
versus **generalization** — inferring answers it does not (hard). A deployed system
needs both: entailment is your regression test (a model that cannot even traverse
what it was shown is broken plumbing), generalization is the product. The leakage
flavor du jour: sampling test queries by running templates over the *full* graph, so
most sampled answers happen to be easy — your "reasoning benchmark" quietly became a
recall benchmark, and a plain database would score honorably on it. Same disease as
Week 3's walks-across-test-edges and Week 4's inverse relations; third costume. In
Lab 5 you will compute the easy/hard gap yourself — expect it to be embarrassingly
large, and to permanently change how you read reasoning leaderboards.

## 4. The LLM era, part one: structure as a retrieval index

Language models made knowledge graphs front-page infrastructure, through a
back door: **retrieval**. An LLM answering from your documents needs the right context
in its window; vanilla RAG retrieves the top-$k$ chunks whose embeddings resemble the
question. For single-fact questions that works. For the questions this lecture is
about, it fails structurally — resemblance is not connection:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w5-graphrag.html >}}

Before the fix, be precise about the disease, because "RAG fails on multi-hop" is
folklore until you can name the mechanism. Vector retrieval embeds the *whole
question* as one point and returns chunks near it. A two-hop question's evidence
lives in two chunks, each containing *half* the question's vocabulary — so each
scores mediocre similarity, while some single chunk that superficially resembles the
full question (same entities, same register, wrong facts) outscores both. The
failure is architectural, not a matter of better embeddings: one query point cannot
be simultaneously near two texts that are not near each other — the exact geometry
lesson as "why not points" in §2, replayed at the document level. (You could retrieve
more chunks and hope; $k$ large enough to catch hop two also drowns the context in
lookalikes, and the model's attention becomes your retrieval system — expensively.)
Decomposing the question into sub-queries helps and is widely done; but sub-query
decomposition over text is just multi-hop traversal with extra steps and no
guarantees — at which point one asks for the structure explicitly.

**GraphRAG** is the family of fixes that put a KG between the corpus and the model:
<span class="term" data-def="Entity linking: mapping a mention in text ('IU', 'the university') to the KG node it denotes. The entry point of every GraphRAG query — and its most common point of failure.">link
the question's entities</span>, retrieve the relevant *subgraph* (neighborhoods,
paths between linked entities), and hand the LLM **facts with provenance** instead of
lookalike paragraphs. Everything you learned this fortnight slots into that sentence:
the subgraph retrieval is Week 5 §1's traversal (with completion optionally
sweetening it), the KG's quality is Week 4's whole curriculum, and the linker is the
new component whose failure modes get their own pitfall below. Microsoft's GraphRAG — this week's required reading — goes
further for corpus-level "sensemaking" questions: an LLM extracts an entity graph
from the whole corpus, **Leiden community detection** (Week 2, taking a bow in
production) partitions it hierarchically, communities get pre-computed summaries, and
a global question is answered map-reduce over community summaries. "What are the main
themes of this corpus?" is unanswerable by any top-$k$ chunk retrieval — no chunk
contains the corpus — and becomes tractable when the corpus has been given a
structure to summarize along.

Since GraphRAG is the thing many of you will actually build at work, open the hood
properly. The **indexing pipeline** — run once per corpus, refreshed incrementally —
has four stages, each with a cost profile worth knowing before you promise a
timeline. (1) *Extraction*: an LLM reads every chunk and emits entities and typed
relations; this is the expensive stage — one-to-several model calls per chunk, so a
100k-document corpus is a real budget line, and the reason teams cache aggressively
and version their extraction prompts like code. (2) *Canonicalization*: merge the
mention-level entities into stable nodes (§5 is entirely about what goes wrong
here). (3) *Community structure*: Leiden over the entity graph, hierarchically —
communities of communities — giving the corpus a table of contents it never had.
(4) *Summarization*: an LLM writes a summary per community, bottom-up, each level
summarizing the level below. The result is a queryable artifact at several
granularities: raw chunks, entities with their subgraphs, and community summaries.

**Query time** then has two distinct modes, and conflating them is the most common
GraphRAG misunderstanding. **Local search** serves entity-anchored questions — link
the question's entities, pull their neighborhoods plus attached source chunks, hand
the bundle to the model; latency is comparable to vector RAG since the graph hops
are index lookups. **Global search** serves corpus-level questions — "what are the
recurring themes?" — by map-reducing over community summaries: ask the question of
each relevant summary (map), synthesize the partial answers (reduce). It is slower
and costs several model calls, which is fine, because the questions it serves were
previously *impossible* rather than slow. The routing rule from the bake-off now has
three branches: entity-anchored → local; corpus-global → global; neither → plain
vector retrieval. And a fourth, quietly load-bearing capability falls out of the
architecture for free: **provenance surfaces through the graph** — every retrieved
fact carries its source chunk, so answers arrive with citations a user can audit,
which for regulated deployments is not a feature but the requirement that got the
project funded.

How do you know any of it works? RAG evaluation decomposes into two questions that
must be measured separately, because they fail independently. **Retrieval quality**:
did the needed evidence reach the context? — the *coverage* metric you will compute
in the lab (against gold supporting facts), plus ranking metrics when the gold is
graded. **Faithfulness**: did the generated answer actually follow from the
retrieved evidence, or did the model freelance? — measured by entailment checks of
answer claims against retrieved sources, human-audited on samples. The Microsoft
paper's own evaluation — LLM-as-judge rating "comprehensiveness" and "diversity" —
measures neither directly, which the required reading asks you to critique; the
critique writes itself once you have the decomposition. Cost enters honestly too: a
GraphRAG index is worth building when the corpus is queried *many times* (the
indexing cost amortizes — the same economics as Query2box's amortized reasoning, one
section ago) and when multi-hop or global questions are a real fraction of traffic;
for a corpus queried twice, vector RAG's zero-index-cost wins on arithmetic alone.

Honesty about the other direction: when the question has no linkable entity, or the
KG is sparse where the question lives, similarity wins — fuzzy questions are vector
RAG's home turf. Production systems route; the bake-off below is
small enough to referee by hand and real enough that both sides win somewhere:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w5-rag.html >}}

## 5. Part two: the model builds the graph

Where do KGs come from? For decades the answers were curation (expensive, precise,
slow — Wikidata's volunteer army; the pharma companies' teams of biocurators) and
classical information extraction (pattern-based, brittle, cheap). The 2020s answer is
LLMs reading text — extraction quality that pattern systems never reached, at a price
per document that keeps falling — which closes a strange loop (models building the
structure that grounds models) and inherits every classic information-extraction
failure at new scale, now delivered with perfect grammar and total confidence. The
three failures you will meet in the first hour of any real project:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w5-construction.html >}}

1. **Canonicalization.** "IU", "Innopolis University", "the university" — extraction
   mints a new entity per surface form, and your graph's entity count inflates with
   aliases. Every downstream join silently fragments: the completion model sees two
   half-connected universities where reality has one, the query engine finds paths
   through neither, and coverage metrics *overstate* the graph (more entities!) while
   its usefulness quietly falls. Repairs: alias resolution against a gazetteer,
   embedding-based entity matching, and *schema-first* extraction (force the model to
   link to existing IDs, not to invent strings).
2. **Precision.** Extractors hallucinate fluent, plausible, false triples — and a KG
   *launders* them: once a fact is a crisp triple with a URI, it looks exactly as
   authoritative as a curated one. The laundering is the dangerous part — text keeps
   its hedges ("reportedly", "some claim"), a triple keeps nothing. Repair: keep
   **provenance** (source span per triple) as a mandatory schema field, and verify
   samples against sources.
3. **Schema drift.** Free extraction invents relations (*located_in*, *situated_in*,
   *lies_in*…) and violates type signatures — three spellings of one relation
   fragment your relation statistics the way aliases fragment entities, and every
   Week-4 pattern audit silently breaks. Repair: extract *into* a fixed ontology
   with type-checking — Week 1's "modeling decision" doctrine, enforced by a
   validator.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w5-extract.html >}}

The widget's three toggles each stand for a real engineering literature; here is the
minimum a practitioner should know about each. **Canonicalization at scale** is a
matching problem with a quadratic temptation: you cannot compare every mention to
every entity, so production systems *block* first (cheap keys — normalized names,
initial letters, embedding-space buckets — that shortlist candidates), then *match*
within blocks using string similarity, attribute agreement, and increasingly an
embedding of the mention's *context* (the same trick as Week 3: things are known by
their company — two mentions with matching neighborhoods are the same entity). The
newest twist is using the LLM itself as the matcher ("are these the same
institution?"), which works embarrassingly well and fails exactly where it matters
most: confident merging of similarly-named distinct entities (two "St. Mary's
Hospital"s), the one error class worse than duplication, because merges destroy
information while duplicates merely dilute it. Bias the pipeline toward
under-merging; duplicates can be fixed tomorrow. **Schema-first extraction** means
the prompt carries the ontology — allowed relation list, type signatures, and
required output format — turning the model from an author into a form-filler;
measured extraction precision routinely jumps double digits versus free-form
prompting, and the rejected residue ("interesting non-conforming facts") becomes the
queue for deliberate schema evolution rather than accidental drift. **Verification
economics** is the uncomfortable one: you cannot afford to verify everything, so
spend the audit budget where queries land — sample per *relation type* (error rates
vary wildly by relation), audit the high-traffic entities disproportionately, and
wire the provenance field so that end-user corrections flow back as labeled data.
A KG built this way gets *more* trustworthy with use; one built without provenance
can only decay.

The loop's moral, which is also this course's KG arc in one sentence: **extraction is
cheap now; trust is the product.** Canonicalization, verification, and provenance are
where the engineering lives — and a GraphRAG system is only as good as the graph you
feed it (the widget's red box is what "confidently wrong" looks like at retrieval
time).

### The three-body problem, named

Zoom out once before the pitfalls, because the two halves of the LLM era — §4 and §5
— are instances of a taxonomy worth carrying whole (it organizes this week's optional
roadmap survey, and more usefully, it organizes vendor pitches). Systems combining
KGs and LLMs come in three patterns. **KG-enhanced LLM**: the graph serves the model
— GraphRAG, KG-grounded prompting, structured tool use; the KG's job is precision
and provenance, the model's job is language. **LLM-augmented KG**: the model serves
the graph — extraction, canonicalization, schema suggestion, even embedding-model
training data; the model's job is coverage, the KG's job is to be the durable,
auditable artifact. **Synergized**: the loop closed deliberately — the model builds
and repairs the graph that grounds it, with verification gates at the interface
(Q7 below stress-tests exactly this pattern's failure mode). When someone shows you
an architecture diagram with a graph and a language model in it, your first question
now has a name: *which of the three is this, and where are the gates?* Most
production systems today are the first pattern with aspirations toward the third;
knowing the difference between the aspiration and the gate is due diligence.

One more placement note for your mental map of the field: everything this week
reasoned over a *fixed* vocabulary of entities and relations — Query2box's anchors
are still table lookups (Week 3's transductive wall, unbroken since). The frontier
beyond this course's core: *inductive* reasoners like ULTRA (optional reading)
that transfer zero-shot to unseen KGs by embedding relations relative to each other
rather than absolutely — one pretrained reasoner for any graph. Read it after Week 6
and you will recognize the trick as message passing over a graph *of relations*;
the two halves of this course are about to start compounding.

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 1 · Answering multi-hop questions by chaining lookups" icon="false"}
The failure is quantitative, so hold the numbers: per-hop reliability compounds
($0.9^3 \approx 0.73$) and intermediate frontiers explode ($b^k$). If your system
design contains "then, for each candidate, query again", you are building the thing
§1 buried. Either embed the query, or bound the depth and own the error bar — and
note the modern costume this pitfall wears: an LLM agent calling a search tool in a
loop *is* chained lookup, with the same compounding and a language model's
confidence stapled on top. The analysis of §1 applies to agentic retrieval
unchanged, which makes it strangely current for mathematics this simple.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 2 · Reasoning benchmarks that a database would ace" icon="false"}
If test answers are reachable by traversing training edges, you are measuring recall,
not inference. Demand the easy/hard split in anything you read; compute it in
anything you build; and when a system must serve both, report both channels — a
model strong on generalization and weak on entailment is broken differently, not
better. (Leakage trilogy now complete: walks over test edges, inverse triples,
traversable answers — all one disease: test information flowing through the data
pipeline.)
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 3 · GraphRAG on a rotten graph" icon="false"}
Structured retrieval adds an authority veneer: the LLM receives crisp triples and
cites them confidently — including the hallucinated ones (Figure 4's red box). A
GraphRAG system inherits its KG's precision *and hides it*: end users see citations,
which read as verification, which is precisely what an unverified extraction is not.
Before routing questions to the graph, audit extraction precision on a sample, and
surface provenance to the end user, not just to the model — a citation that opens
the actual source span is worth ten precision points of trust.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 4 · Treating entity linking as solved" icon="false"}
The bake-off's fuzzy question failed graph retrieval for one reason: nothing in it
linked. Real questions are full of pronouns, nicknames, and descriptions ("the
Kazan-based university"); linking recall bounds everything downstream. Measure it
separately — a perfect subgraph retriever behind a 60% linker is a 60% system. And
resist the tempting fix of maximally aggressive linking: over-eager linkers that
match every capitalized phrase pull in wrong subgraphs, and a *wrong* subgraph is
worse than none, because the downstream model treats retrieved structure as
authoritative (Pitfall 3's veneer, self-inflicted). Precision and recall of the
linker deserve their own dashboard, per entity type, before any end-to-end number
is worth discussing.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 5 · Believing the box (or the beta)" icon="false"}
Query embeddings return *plausible* regions, not certified answers: the box that
generously recovered Naproxen will, on another query, generously include garbage —
and unlike a traversal engine, it cannot show you the path it took, because there
was none. There is no free calibration under the open-world assumption (Week 4,
still true), and there is no free explanation either. For decisions that matter,
treat query-embedding output as a candidate generator feeding verification — a
shortlist for the traversal engine, the curator, or the lab — never as an oracle.
:::

## In this week's lab

[Lab 5](../labs/lab05.qmd) builds both halves of the lecture. Half one: Query2box-lite
from scratch — the box distance, the projection and intersection operators (each
against hand-checkable asserts), trained on FB15k-237 queries, evaluated with the
easy/hard split so you can watch a "reasoning" metric collapse when the lookups are
taken away. Half two: a mini-GraphRAG over a small document set — entity linking,
subgraph retrieval, and the coverage metric from Figure 3, head-to-head against
cosine retrieval on one-hop, two-hop, and fuzzy questions — no API keys, the "LLM" is
whoever reads the retrieved context, which for grading purposes is you.

One lab war story is worth telling in advance, because it is a lecture point wearing
overalls. The first draft of the training loop taught the box operators from 2-hop
path samples alone — and hard-answer Hits@10 sat at random. Diagnosis: FB15k-237 has
237 relations, and a few thousand sampled paths cannot teach 237 projection
operators their geometry; the fix was to pretrain every relation's operator on plain
1-hop queries — that is, on *all of Week 4* — before fine-tuning on paths. The
shipped lab keeps both phases, labeled, and the general lesson is compositional
learning's quiet prerequisite: operators compose only if each operator was learnable
*alone* from enough data. When your fancy compositional system underperforms,
check whether its atoms ever got trained.

## Required reading

**1 · Ren, Hu & Leskovec — *Query2box: Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs in Vector Space using Box Embeddings* (ICLR 2020).** [arXiv:2002.05969](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05969)

::: {.reading-annotation}
The week's core method. Study Figures 1–2 — the query computation graph and the box
operators — until you can trace a 2-hop query end to end, then read how the DNF
rewrite smuggles unions into a conjunction-only geometry. Note the evaluation:
generalization is measured on answers *requiring* held-out edges — §3's protocol, at
the source. Skim the theoretical remarks and the hyperparameter appendix.
:::

**2 · Edge et al. — *From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization* (2024).** [arXiv:2404.16130](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130)

::: {.reading-annotation}
The Microsoft GraphRAG paper. Focus on the pipeline figure — LLM extraction → entity
graph → **Leiden** communities (wave to Week 2) → hierarchical summaries → map-reduce
answering — and on *why* top-$k$ chunk retrieval cannot answer corpus-level
questions. Then read the evaluation critically: LLM-as-judge on "comprehensiveness"
and "diversity" is the weakest link — articulate what a sturdier evaluation would
measure. Skim the prompt-engineering appendix.
:::

**Also see:** Hamilton, *GRL book*, §4.5 (compositional reasoning) · CS224W,
"Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs".

**Optional:** Ren & Leskovec, [BetaE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11465) (NeurIPS
2020) — negation via Beta distributions; read Figure 1 and the negation operator as a
case study in geometry-follows-operators · Sun et al.,
[A Re-evaluation of KG Completion Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.03903) (ACL
2020) — reread from Week 4, now as a reasoning-evaluation cautionary tale · Pan et
al., [Unifying LLMs and KGs: A Roadmap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08302) (2024) —
navigate by the taxonomy figure; place GraphRAG and §5 in it; mine the bibliography
for project ideas · Galkin et al., [ULTRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04562) (ICLR
2024) — one pretrained reasoner, zero-shot on 50+ unseen KGs; ask what "inductive"
means here vs. in Query2box.

## Check your understanding

<details><summary>Q1 · Formalize — Write the analyst's query "companies owned by subsidiaries of sanctioned entities" as a conjunctive query with quantifiers, draw its computation DAG in words, and mark where an intersection would appear if we add "…and headquartered in the EU".</summary>
$q(C) = \exists S, E:\; \textit{sanctioned}(E) \wedge \textit{subsidiary\_of}(S, E)
\wedge \textit{owned\_by}(C, S)$. DAG: anchor set (sanctioned entities) →
subsidiary_of⁻¹ → variable $S$ → owned_by⁻¹ → answer variable $C$. Adding the HQ
constraint creates a second branch anchored at EU — $\textit{hq\_in}(C, \text{EU})$
— meeting the first at $C$: that meeting point is the intersection operator, and in
Query2box it is where two boxes shrink to their overlap.
</details>

<details><summary>Q2 · The two deaths — A 4-hop query; per-hop completion reliability 0.85; average branching 50. Compute the chained pipeline's end-to-end reliability and its frontier size at the last hop, then state in one sentence each how query embedding avoids both.</summary>
Reliability $0.85^4 \approx 0.52$ — a coin flip. Frontier $\approx 50^3 = 125{,}000$
candidate paths entering hop 4 (the first hop starts from one anchor). Query
embedding never enumerates intermediates — depth is a sequence of operator
applications on one region ($O(k)$ matrix ops) — and it does not multiply per-hop
error probabilities because no intermediate *decision* is taken: softness is carried
in the region until the single final scoring step.
</details>

<details><summary>Q3 · Geometry follows operators — Your product needs queries with conjunction and negation ("protein pairs that interact AND are not both membrane-bound"). Using @prp-closure, explain why Query2box cannot host this natively, what BetaE changes, and the general design rule.</summary>
Boxes close under intersection but the complement of a box is not a box — negation
exits the representation class, and no parameterization fixes that (it is geometry,
not capacity; same *shape* of argument as DistMult's forced symmetry in Week 4).
BetaE represents queries as products of Beta distributions, where complement is the
parameter swap $(\alpha, \beta) \to (\beta, \alpha)$ — closed, cheap, differentiable.
Rule: enumerate the logical operators your application needs *first*, then choose a
geometry closed under all of them. Representation before architecture.
</details>

<details><summary>Q4 · Easy vs hard — A benchmark reports Hits@3 = 0.61 for 2-hop queries. You discover 78% of test answers are traversable in the training graph, where the system scores 0.74; on the rest it scores h. Compute h, and write the one-sentence review comment you would leave.</summary>
$0.61 = 0.78 \times 0.74 + 0.22 \times h \Rightarrow h = (0.61 - 0.577)/0.22 \approx
0.15$. Comment: "The headline number is three-quarters database recall; on answers
that require inference the system scores ≈0.15, which is the paper's actual
contribution and should be the abstract's number — please report the easy/hard split
(Query2box protocol) throughout." (The arithmetic habit of decomposing a metric by
subpopulation is Week 4's stratify-by-frequency pitfall, promoted to queries.)
</details>

<details><summary>Q5 · Routing — For each question, pick vector RAG, GraphRAG (subgraph), or GraphRAG (community summaries), with one clause of justification: (a) "What did the 2019 contract say about penalties?" (b) "Which suppliers depend, directly or indirectly, on factories in region X?" (c) "What are the recurring risk themes across all our audit reports?" (d) "Something about that clause with the weird wording…"</summary>
(a) Vector RAG — single-document fact, similarity suffices. (b) GraphRAG subgraph —
"directly or indirectly" is a path query over a dependency graph; similarity cannot
compose hops. (c) GraphRAG community summaries — a corpus-global sensemaking question;
no chunk contains the answer (the Microsoft paper's home case). (d) Vector RAG — no
linkable entity, pure fuzziness; entity linking would return nothing (Pitfall 4).
Scoring pattern: hops → subgraph; global → communities; neither → similarity.
</details>

<details><summary>Q6 · The rotten graph — Your GraphRAG pilot answers confidently and cites triples, and spot-checks find 8% of cited triples are extraction hallucinations. Name the three-part repair from §5, ordered by expected impact, and say which part the *user interface* must carry.</summary>
(1) Provenance as a mandatory field, surfaced in the UI — every answer links the
source span, so a wrong triple is one click from exposure (the UI part: users must
see sources, not just the model). (2) Verification pass: sample-audit extraction
against sources, gate low-confidence triples out of retrieval (or label them).
(3) Canonicalization + schema type-checking to kill the alias/typing fraction of
errors mechanically. Impact order can be argued, but provenance leads because it
converts silent errors into detectable ones — it repairs the *system's
epistemology*, not just its precision.
</details>

<details><summary>Q7 · The loop — An LLM extracts a KG from a corpus; a GraphRAG system over that KG then grounds the same LLM's answers about the corpus. Give one reason this loop is genuinely better than the LLM alone, and one failure mode where the loop amplifies rather than fixes hallucination — plus the guard rail.</summary>
Better: the KG is a *checkable intermediate* — extraction happens once, can be
audited, deduplicated, type-checked and given provenance, so answer-time generation
is constrained by a vetted structure instead of free recall (and multi-hop questions
become traversals, which LLMs are bad at doing implicitly). Amplifies: an extraction
hallucination becomes a crisp, citable triple that the same model later retrieves as
"evidence" — self-grounding on its own confabulation, with the authority veneer of
Pitfall 3. Guard rail: never let a triple into retrieval without a source span, and
verify a sample of high-impact relations against those spans (trust budget spent
where queries actually land).
</details>

## Where this leaves us

The knowledge-graph arc of this course is complete: facts as geometry (Week 4),
questions as geometry (today), and the 2020s realignment — graphs as the trust layer
under language models, and language models as the assembly line for graphs. You can
now formalize a multi-hop question, embed it, grade the answer without grading a
database, and route between structure and similarity like someone who has seen both
fail.

The arc also completes a quieter education in *design method* that is worth stating
once, explicitly, as the thing to carry out of these two weeks even if every model
name fades. Three times running, the winning move was the same: write down the
operations your problem requires, then choose a representation closed under them —
directed facts demanded asymmetric scorers, composition demanded a relation group,
conjunction demanded intersectable regions, negation demanded mirrorable
distributions. And three times running, the field's honest evaluators had to invent
a split that separated *memory* from *inference* — filtered ranking, hard answers,
leakage audits — because the naive metric flattered recall. Representation follows
operators; evaluation separates memory from inference. Two sentences, and they will
serve you in corners of ML that have never heard of a knowledge graph. When a new
benchmark or model reaches you, run both tests in that order — what are the
operators, and what does the split actually separate — and you will usually know a
paper's worth before you reach its experiments section.

Notice, though, what every method since Week 3 has had in common: the encoder is
still a **table**. DeepWalk looked vectors up; TransE looked vectors up; even
Query2box looks up its anchors. Week 3's four walls still stand — no parameter
sharing, no new entities, and, most painfully: all those node *features* — the
paper's words, the protein's sequence, the account's profile — still lying on the
floor, untouched since Lab 2. Next week the table is finally replaced by a machine:
an encoder that *computes* a node's vector from its features and its neighbors'
features, recursively — and every thread of the first five weeks converges on it.
The Laplacian you met in Week 1 becomes its propagation matrix; the label
propagation of Week 3 becomes its ancestor; the aggregation instinct of this week's
intersection operator becomes its defining move; and the WL algorithm of Week 2 is
waiting, four weeks downstream, to tell it what it can never see. You have already
peeked at its page — Week 6 has been published since the course began, as a promise
of where this was going. Now you have every prerequisite it assumes. The graph
neural network era of this course starts Thursday.
